entities.name: Kubernetes
entities.desc:
Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration and cluster-management platform used in cloud, managed, on-premises, and infrastructure environments, including Amazon EKS, Google GKE, Nebius, JetBrains infrastructure, and custom deployment consoles. It provides cluster control planes, APIs, worker nodes, scheduling, service discovery, namespaces, and workload execution for production applications, scheduled jobs, ETL, highly available services, machine-learning pipelines, databases, Kafka, ClickHouse, TeamCity, Kubeflow, monitoring systems, and other workloads. It also hosts macOS virtual machines managed by icri as pods and serves as the upstream platform for a macOS-patched kubelet fork.

Kubernetes organizes clusters and namespaces containing pods, containers, Deployments, Jobs, CronJobs, Services, Ingresses, PersistentVolumeClaims, volumes, ConfigMaps, Secrets, ServiceAccounts, quotas, LimitRanges, NetworkPolicies, runtime classes, and storage. It supports declarative manifests, custom resources, controllers, and operators; rolling updates, retries for failed Jobs, autoscaling, resource allocation, affinity and topology rules, GPU workloads, node labels and taints, eviction, health probes, lifecycle management, scheduling, and configurable runtime behavior. Supported runtimes include containerd and Kata Containers, while external access may use load balancers, ExternalName Services, ingress controllers, TLS, and external-dns.

Kubernetes is the operating platform for the Database Controller, Kafka Controller, Object Storage Controller, and other custom controllers, and integrates with systems such as GitHub Controller, Strimzi, External Secrets Operator, ArgoCD, Karpenter, and ClickHouse operators. It is also associated with Kafka-controller documentation, custom resource definitions, kubeconfig contexts, and Helm-managed objects.

Administration uses `kubectl`, kubeconfig, APIs, and custom consoles, with RBAC, auditing, impersonation, VPN-restricted APIs, service authorization, and private registry support. Observability and troubleshooting use events, logs, tracing, metrics APIs, PodMonitors, exporters, alerts, and related tools. Kubernetes documentation references version 1.22 or later as an upstream compatibility boundary and permits a kubelet to lag its control plane by up to three minor versions.

In related configuration and documentation contexts, Kubernetes is the cluster platform in which Deployments, pods, namespaces, NetworkPolicies, events, PersistentVolumeClaims, ingresses, and nodes operate or are investigated. It is also referenced as a skill with test namespaces recorded through `kubectl`, an older file format containing a section from which test namespaces are extracted, and a keyword associated with networking-configuration retrieval and infrastructure-focused example queries.<SEP>Kubernetes is the subject of the example question used with the memory recall command.<SEP>Kubernetes is the platform context for the Ingress, Service, and load-balancing configuration described in the document.<SEP>Kubernetes provides the annotation mechanism used to configure ALB access-log export.

entities.name: ZenML
entities.desc:
ZenML is an ML and data-pipeline orchestration platform and a running company-wide AI tooling service for developers. It provides the pipeline runner, user interface, and Kubernetes sandbox integration used by implementations such as the LME / AI Assistant and the JetBrains SWE-eval pipeline. In the latter, ZenML is delegated responsibility for creating pods. ZenML generally runs one Kubernetes Job or individual pod per pipeline step, including the `swe_harbor` pipeline and its associated orchestrator Jobs.

ZenML manages pipeline artifacts and storage: pipeline steps write artifacts to a shared GCS artifact bucket, while its MySQL database stores artifact URIs. It is also an external or third-party tool that can connect to GKE through a DNS endpoint, access a Kubernetes cluster, and register an artifact store. Connectors for Crusoe and GKE are being developed, and ZenML is associated with a cross-cluster connector reference implementation. A dedicated cluster in `gke-europe-west1` runs its GPU pipeline steps.

ZenML is also the workload environment and named namespace involved in several Kubernetes and infrastructure contexts. Its shared or affected node pools were involved in the ComputeClass rollout, including ComputeClass taints. Its node-selector and toleration settings determine Kubernetes sandbox placement; sandbox pods receive selectable session labels and use the sandbox environment’s egress controls. The `swe_harbor` execution path has experienced transient sandbox connectivity failures, and ZenML is associated with two independent failure classes and serves as a comparison point for a partially documented path.

Operationally, ZenML is an internal service whose network access may motivate use of `sre-eqx-kata`. A permanently running Junie Slack-bot agent was intended to provide access to ZenML, and ZenML is the system accessed through that agent. ZenML also confirmed operation with a workaround using an external Ingress and static hosts entry. It was the named namespace in a high-cardinality Prometheus out-of-memory incident. In an application or owning-team context, ZenML was associated with changing a Cloud SQL instance from `db-custom-4-15360` to Enterprise Plus `db-perf-optimized-N-4`.<SEP>ZenML is associated with the swe_harbor implementation of the harbor agent-evaluation framework.<SEP>ZenML is listed as a Managed Service associated with ZenML OSS / AI+ML4SE teams.

entities.name: SRE
entities.desc:
SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) is JetBrains’ infrastructure and service-reliability function, organizational group, operational team, YouTrack project and issue namespace, support channel, and knowledge area. It supports most listed products and managed services according to the assigned engagement, identifies ownership in YouTrack, receives Prometheus health alerts and controller failures routed through `ctrlReconcileError`, and handles onboarding, documentation, requests, incidents, alerts, postmortems, access, deployments, build agents, OAuth, Grafana, CodeSign, infrastructure, synchronization boards, goals, methodologies, and SRE principles. It is also one side of the support split for skills and provides system-level support for the site, search, indexer, CLI, and installers. Individual members may act as Kubernetes administrators or human operators.

SRE operates and develops the platforms used to launch and maintain company services, including Kubernetes environments on Hetzner, Nebius, GKE, EKS, on-premises, and other clouds, with GPU and untrusted-workload capacity. Its tooling and infrastructure include CoreDNS, ArgoCD/GitOps, cert-manager, ingress, Karpenter, gVisor, monitoring, Loki, Grafana, AlertManager, CloudArmor, registry caching, TeamCity, Langfuse, LiteLLM, agent images, and related Terraform, Pulumi, AMI, and infrastructure repositories. Loki is available to SRE personnel without namespace access restrictions. Since August 2026, SRE has owned and supported LiteLLM and Langfuse, with Langfuse ownership specifically confirmed.

SRE creates and owns dedicated infrastructure and servers in SRE GCP/AWS projects, receives their alerts, manages scaling, and handles dedicated-database server procedures. It confirms and provisions requested database instances, including RDS/PostgreSQL and dedicated databases, and investigates failures, networking and cache problems, stuck pods and jobs, quotas, capacity, migrations, cleanup, controlled restoration, and second-database provisioning. It manages namespaces, node pools, cluster policies, DNS, certificates, Route53 zones, selected domains, firewall and routing rules, production issuers, authentication projects, OAuth redirect URIs, Workload Identity Federation, incident-dump storage, and shared-subnet arrangements.

SRE provisions or approves IAM and trust bindings, Kubernetes roles and RBAC, Google Groups, namespaces, registry credentials, runners, ingress, Kafka resources, and quota increases. It maintains reference Helm charts, shared macOS agents, selected GitHub runners, authentication scripts, images, labels, dashboards, inventories, and security-review evidence; some GitHub-managed runner requests are redirected to ADM. Namespace administrators may manage QuotaClaim, while SRE edits QuotaLimit and GCSBucket configuration when required and can grant increases beyond defaults.

Its authority is limited by ReadOnlyAccess, elevated-access requirements, CI pipelines, formal approvals, and owner approval for writes or policy exceptions. SRE does not own corporate AWS governance, Transit Gateway, organization policies, Access Context Manager, certain accounts or secrets, Microsoft Azure management, Trino support, tenant-controlled configuration, some IP allowlists, or the receiving side of the Grazie pipeline. It does not support team-owned server-side issues, does not enforce Security-team approval, and provides cluster guidance through `#sre`, including ingress choices. It handles cert-manager zone changes, recommends Gateway API as the long-term replacement, has confirmed a Thanos incompatibility, and announces Thanos upgrades.

entities.name: Tenant
entities.desc:
Tenant is a context-dependent concept used in observability, application management, configuration, metrics, and shared database operations. In metrics systems, a tenant defines a data partition, with its blocks stored under a tenant-specific path; in expected-usage metrics, “tenant” is a label identifying the relevant usage scope. In Grafana Tempo, it is an isolated tracing environment that can be connected to a Grafana organization. In Loki, it is a log-isolation boundary identified by an organization ID and used to control log access, and may also denote a separate Loki tenancy for logs originating from a team’s own infrastructure.

In application operations, a tenant represents the customer environment being administered or tested, including its namespace, resources, database, access configuration, and user interface. Recovery procedures may involve the tenant’s database, URL, namespace, operating mode, and master secret. After the tenant’s project exists, the tenant places Application manifests in its own repository and can opt an Application into notifications by adding subscription annotations there. A tenant can also create an instance custom resource corresponding to a matching pre-baked custom resource definition.

In configuration, Tenant is a referenced category for external-service push tenants. Such a tenant may be identified by a string name and receive explicit ingestion-limit overrides through `per_tenant_overrides`.

In shared-database contexts, a tenant is a consumer or occupant of a database on a shared PostgreSQL instance. It cannot independently select a different major database version, may encounter a public-schema permission error after an upgrade, and is responsible for arranging finer-grained backups when the shared-instance defaults are insufficient.<SEP>A tenant is an owner whose resources must not be silently adopted or collided with by a different tenant after namespace recreation.<SEP>Tenant is a workload owner whose pod can be affected when shared node-local disk fills.

entities.name: jip-controller
entities.desc:
jip-controller is an internal Kubernetes controller and platform component, also referred to as the JIP Controller, responsible for namespace-lifecycle automation and related cluster operations. Its main reconciler runs with four workers and ordinarily treats user namespaces as managed namespaces. It is deployed on clusters with namespace self-service configuration, including EKS, GKE, GKE Autopilot, Nebius, and hub clusters, as a base, cluster, or SRE platform component. It is absent outside the SRE platform and runs on the hub from 2026-09-14.

The controller reconciles namespaces, owner annotations, baseline policies, RoleBindings, quotas, limits, admission webhooks, and related resources. It applies namespace objects, removes namespace-owner annotations afterward, creates namespace-owner bindings, renders tenant RBAC rules, and supplies per-user RBAC templates and namespace-creation permissions for configured administrators and allowed creators. It supports owner-scoped namespaces without requiring cluster-wide `rolebindings: create` permission. Namespace creation is constrained through mutating and validating webhooks, while Ingress hosts are validated. Its ServiceAccount has `jip-controller`, `user`, and `view` permissions. Username case is preserved through `GetRBSubjectName`; people and robots are distinguished using the `system:` prefix and a named CI service-account exception. The controller emits Kubernetes subject kinds and synchronization events, and its machinery automation excludes the `cilium-secrets` namespace.

jip-controller manages `QuotaClaim` and `QuotaLimit` custom resources and their webhooks, provides default self-service templates, creates `ResourceQuota` objects named `jip-quota`, updates their `spec` and `spec.hard` fields, supplies GCPProject quota profiles, and supports quota synchronization through mechanisms including `ignore-quota-sync`. It configures namespace `LimitRange` objects, including ephemeral-storage constraints for Develocity Reporting Kit components. Its presence determines whether the default channel-annotation policy is available; it formerly set the monitoring namespace channel annotation out of band.

The controller synchronizes Google Group membership into namespace access by impersonating a Google service account, retrieving group members, resolving owner annotations, and writing RoleBindings. This process requires suitable RBAC permissions, uses cached Google Workspace API state, produces central `RoleBindingSyncer` logs, and may require a pod restart after synchronization failure. Helm automatically rolls out the pod when the rendered Google credential ConfigMap changes.

The name also denotes the Kubernetes namespace associated with the `jip-webhook` deployment, which is used to inspect `MAX_NAMESPACE`, as well as `jip-namespaces-owners` configuration, queue and work-duration metrics, and deployment documentation. The component is included in the `kubernetes-pods` job allowlist and Kubernetes pod relabeling regex, and is documented under components and SRE cluster automation. It is associated with worker deployments, reporting components, cluster-wide `namespaces-exporter` RBAC, EKS-only WAFv2 aggregate permissions, default namespace RBAC for `wafv2.services.k8s.aws`, and Argo CD and ArgoProjects self-service configurations.

entities.name: Job
entities.desc:
Job has two distinct meanings in the descriptions. In GitHub Actions, a Job is an executing unit of a workflow that may continue running even when it produces no new log output.

In Kubernetes, a Job is a batch workload resource, typically created by a client, CronJob, terminal, Helm chart, ZenML runner, or other orchestrator. Its job controller creates Pods from the specified pod template, and it represents one-time or background execution. Jobs may be suspended, deleted, waited on, or managed through Jobs/CronJobs; they are also covered by Kyverno policy auto-generation and may pass through the Kueue mutating admission webhook for `batch/v1` creation. A listener may detect a Job while a runner Pod pulls and executes it, and each pipeline task or unit of work may become a quota-tracked Job.

A Kubernetes Job can run database backup, restore, synchronization, or JMX-related operations. It may launch PostgreSQL backup or restore containers, write backups to a specified bucket, execute the `pg-backup-mydb` task, or restore PostgreSQL data using configured secrets and a restore command. It is used for individual backup executions, is the only permitted workload type for restoring backups in the described system, and can be configured to disable Istio sidecar injection. Jobs also support specialized workloads, including the `dws-test-job`, a CUDA workload with one Pod, queued-provisioning annotations, an NVIDIA H200 node selector, GPU tolerations, security settings, and a never-restart policy; a terminal-created `kubectl-toolkit` Pod; and a PgBouncer container for a database-proxy session. Proxy Jobs are created in the caller’s namespace, one per active proxy, and named deterministically from the user and database-secret identifier.

Job failure and lifecycle behavior is governed by settings such as `backoffLimit` and `activeDeadlineSeconds`. Failed Pods count toward `backoffLimit`, although failures to create Pods do not; orchestrator-Pod eviction can nevertheless lead to `BackoffLimitExceeded`. Misconfigured completion or cleanup can leave active Jobs accumulating. Jobs and their failed Pods consume namespace quota, including those created by CronJobs or terminals, and retry behavior can cause Failed-Pod accumulation or quota-induced retry deadlocks. A Job may therefore remain active, fail and retry, or require deletion and cleanup to release quota.<SEP>Job is the Kubernetes workload whose default retry behavior can produce up to seven Failed pods when the cronjob chart settings are absent.<SEP>Job is a Kubernetes workload involved in parallel resource creation that can trigger a ResourceQuota conflict.<SEP>A Job is a workload that can participate in parallel bursts, retries, and quota-related deadlocks.<SEP>Job is an applicable workload type for workloads requiring finite execution.<SEP>A job represents an indexing operation whose completion is awaited before retrieving the latest index.

entities.name: Container
entities.desc:
Container is an isolated runtime and workload unit, typically configured by a name and image and running within a Kubernetes pod. It starts a process—often a shell such as `/bin/sh` or `bash`—and can be entered through `kubectl exec` to inspect processes and file descriptors. Containers may run application workloads, test commands, Docker operations, PostgreSQL restore commands, or backup and restore tasks. They are built and launched from Dockerfiles or images, including a macOS test image and an image serving as the source of the `loggo` binary; an application container may be newly created when repository configuration changes and may contain configuration files mapped from Kubernetes objects.

A container can run as root or as a non-root identity, including UID 1000 or a configured UID and group 1030, with `runAsUser` controlling writer identity. It may receive mounted host directories and retain required runtime capabilities; stricter configurations may use the host network. Networking can instead use bridge mode, with access to published ports, and may encounter DNS-resolution or internet-egress failures. The container’s CPU, memory, ephemeral-storage, and network usage can be constrained by cgroups, with resource requests and explicit limits applied, and its metrics are generally collected by default. It can be selected for dashboard or log filtering.

Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes monitor the running workload; the liveness probe is relevant when the listener is lost. The container exposes an exit code, and non-zero termination codes can contribute to a Job’s `backoffLimit`. It writes application messages to standard output, although the container perspective cannot determine whether consecutive lines belong to the same event.

Secrets may be resolved before startup and supplied as environment-variable key-value pairs or mounted secrets. Values read through the environment remain unchanged until the container restarts. Containers launched by Jobs or CronJobs can access specified buckets through a service account or mounted secrets and write backup files there. A container is also a metadata-bearing object used by the Update Container Metadata task and currently stores a pointer to `macvm.VirtualMachineInfo` as virtual-machine metadata.<SEP>The container may continue running the old image after the playbook and can require a manual service restart.

entities.name: Pod
entities.desc:
Pod is a Kubernetes workload and execution unit that runs one or more containers and their associated processes, often serving as a deployable unit comparable to a lightweight virtual machine. Pods may be created directly, but are commonly managed by Jobs, Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs, terminal systems such as JBCC, custom build infrastructure, or other controllers. A Pod should generally not be created as a bare object because it lacks a controller to provide restart, rescheduling, and lifecycle management; it may nevertheless be started or restarted, triggering immediate maintenance-tick and retention processing.

A Pod specification can include application and infrastructure containers, init containers, injected sidecars, private images and pull secrets, commands, environment variables, Secrets, ConfigMaps, mounted credential files, persistent volume claims, ephemeral storage, writable temporary volumes, restart policies, resource requests and limits, labels, annotations, ServiceAccounts, security contexts, privileged or non-root execution, and runtime classes such as gVisor. Identity may be provided through ServiceAccount credentials, Workload Identity, IRSA, OIDC, or assumed roles. Pods can host diverse workloads, including databases, AWS CLI tasks, Debezium, BuildKit, macOS-build, TeamCity agents, testing, uploads, and kubectl tooling.

Pods are scheduled according to resource availability, quotas, node selectors and affinity, taints and tolerations, region, architecture, capacity type, and GPU requirements. They consume `count/pods` quota, including Job attempts and failed CronJob remnants, as well as CPU, memory, storage, and extended-resource quotas. They may remain Pending because of unsatisfied constraints, unavailable nodes or GPUs, PVCs, missing Secrets, or quota limits; architecture mismatches can prevent image execution.

Each Pod provides a shared network namespace and loopback interface, container resource context, and access to network connectivity and published ports. Services and load balancers may route traffic to it, while operators can use port forwarding, `kubectl exec`, debugging commands, logs, `kubectl describe`, and status queries for access and diagnosis. NetworkPolicy rules evaluate Pod traffic, control its network access, and may require `podSelector` or `namespaceSelector` when the Pod is the destination of a dependency rule; database hostnames can be resolved from within a Pod, and verification may be performed from it.

Pods can expose metrics, use Prometheus annotations, and be monitored for readiness, downtime, and application health. Lifecycle failures include image-pull or configuration errors, initialization failures, liveness-probe restarts, admission or mutation failures, `Terminating` states, eviction caused by memory pressure, ephemeral-storage exhaustion, DiskPressure, or node consolidation, and runtime termination timeouts. A Pod may lose network connectivity or remain Running despite application errors; for example, a Pod can become NotReady when a thanos-sidecar runs out of memory.<SEP>A pod is a Kubernetes resource whose logs and runtime state may be inspected during troubleshooting.<SEP>Pod is a cluster workload entity that can be investigated through log collection and runtime state analysis.

entities.name: PVC
entities.desc:
PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim) is a Kubernetes persistent-storage resource that requests a specified capacity and is typically referenced with a mount path. It provides storage for application data, dump files, repository clones, Docker workloads, GCS FUSE mounts, and other persistent or temporary pod requirements. A named PVC can preserve data across Pod restarts and is generally expected to survive node replacement, unlike local NVMe passthrough storage. PVC storage capacity is distinct from a container’s ephemeral-storage limit; it is not constrained by the LimitRange cap, and exhaustion of the volume returns ENOSPC. Provisioned EBS gp3 capacity is billed whether or not it is used.

PVC creation and use may be evaluated against namespace quota keys for PVCs, storage classes, and related resources. Authenticated users may inspect available StorageClasses to support provisioning. PVC metadata is passed through by csi-resizer during volume expansion and accurate resource tagging. PVC usage and inode metrics can be federated from collector Pods. Storage may be backed by SSD persistent volumes with backups, a node’s LVM volume group, or other volume implementations; local-storage PVCs are limited by the free space of a single node’s disk and are bound to a distinct node. A PVC is also part of the required PersistentVolume-plus-PVC mounting configuration.

PVCs can support Docker pull, build, run, `docker exec`, and published ports through `vfs`, although using persistent storage with Docker incurs the cost or limitations of the `overlay2` driver. In another runtime arrangement, PVC storage is delivered through the gofer as a 9p directfs mount. During Pod teardown, the PVC device is unmounted and unmapped.

PVCs may be used as generic ephemeral volumes. In that mode, Kubernetes automatically creates a quota-tracked PVC for a Pod or pipeline task, such as a Harbor `jobs_dir`, and deletes it with the Pod. This supports large JVM heap dumps when `emptyDir` limits are insufficient, avoids the original node-ephemeral-storage eviction pattern when `/tmp` uses a 20Gi volume, and can retain dump files across Pod restarts when configured accordingly. Each Deployment replica may require a PVC for dump storage, with `dump-uploader` detecting and retaining those files.

PVC data can be migrated by copying content from an old claim to a new claim or into a claim in another cluster; the receiving claim may be too large for the described migration process. PVCs considered for synchronization may represent storage-volume pairs. Storage normally persists through routine Helm upgrades and image changes, but may be recreated after manual deletion or changes to an immutable `volumeClaimTemplates` block. Local PVC sizing must fit within one node’s available volume-group space.<SEP>PVC is a Kubernetes object that can use `prometheus.io/service_itm` and `prometheus.io/site` annotations for alert routing.<SEP>PVC is an allowed volume type under restrict-volume-types.<SEP>PVC is a Kubernetes resource whose binding state may be checked during runtime investigation.

entities.name: Namespace
entities.desc:
Namespace is a Kubernetes resource and logical organizational scope within a cluster. It isolates projects, teams, tenants, environments, and workloads, including development, staging, and production, and supports multitenancy with limited system impact. A required Namespace must exist in the target Kubernetes cluster before applications, agent-based services, or applications connecting to Kafka with kafka-controller enabled can be deployed. It is also the naming scope in which object names must be unique and the scope containing application pods, their network resources, and NetworkPolicy resources carried by a raw release.

Namespaces can be created through Cloud Console, the JBCC wizard, CLI or kubectl, Kubeflow, self-service workflows, authorized namespace-creation requests, or the documented JIP Controller workflow. Creation is governed by authorization, naming conventions, project prefixes, cluster or regional quotas, and placement requirements. Subsequent synchronization tools, JIP, webhooks, and Kyverno validation or mutation may provision ownership metadata, default objects, quotas, and optional Kubeflow or other resources.

The Namespace scopes resources including pods, services, ingresses, HTTPRoutes, databases, buckets, topics, CRDs, secrets, workloads, application releases, CI/CD integrations, TeamCity projects, Grafana instances, VKAR objects, Kafka topics and adoption rules, WAFv2 WebACLs, LogsHandlers, PostgreSQL instances, QuotaClaims, SpaceApplications, and GCPProject objects. Kafka resources and KafkaACLBinding references resolve within it, while an S3Bucket custom resource cannot be moved between namespaces. PostgreSQLInstance registration and quota management occur in the Namespace, and its identity must be supplied to SRE when requesting a dedicated database server.

Namespace is the primary boundary for RBAC, ownership, visibility, and controller permissions. Roles, RoleBindings, ServiceAccounts, ResourceGrants, deployment users, and administrator access are assigned within it. Annotations and metadata record owners, teams, channels, emails, and service identifiers; ownership annotations may trigger JIP initialization, while channel annotations determine alert destinations such as Slack.

ResourceQuota, LimitRange, pod, GPU, storage, and quota-claim policies can restrict deployments, jobs, pods, persistent-volume claims, and other workloads, with LimitRange able to inject default pod resources. Namespace-scoped secrets must be uniquely named, and deletion removes them from that scope. Namespaces also provide context for service-mesh injection, monitoring, terminals, logging, auditing, metric scraping, network-resource display, and cost attribution. Network policies—including documented baseline pod-egress restrictions—node selectors, inbound and outbound defaults, tolerations, encryption-key ownership, synchronization exclusions, filtering, and independently managed lifecycles may further constrain behavior. Namespaces may be claimed, transferred, audited, finalized, decommissioned, or deleted after an unclaimed grace period, subject to permissions and cleanup requirements.<SEP>A namespace is a Kubernetes scope that may have access restrictions for kubectl operations.<SEP>A namespace is the Kubernetes scope where exported ALB logs appear with ingress and stream labels.

entities.name: jip-quota
entities.desc:
jip-quota is the conventional default name of a namespace-scoped Kubernetes ResourceQuota object. It is created or provisioned by components such as jip-controller and NamespaceSyncer, and is expected to appear after the namespace synchronization fix. It serves as the per-namespace quota shared by all workloads and carries both configured limits and usage accounting. Instances are associated with namespaces including my-new-namespace, sre-staging, and skills-index.

jip-quota controls admission and resource consumption through `spec.hard` limits and `status.used` counters. It can limit pod counts, memory and other resource requests, and monitoring resources such as `monitoring.coreos.com/samples` and `monitoring.coreos.com/labels`. In skills-index, podmonitor and prometheusrule usage is reported as zero out of a limit of ten. Pod limits can prevent further creation or worker scale-out when requested memory exceeds the remaining ceiling; in one case, the pod limit was reached and remained at ten. Usage is held by running pods, pods in `ImagePullBackOff`, and the terminal’s own Job and pod.

The quota can also act as a per-namespace feature switch governing admission of GCPProject objects. During quota-claim reconciliation, QuotaSyncer applies values from `quotaclaim.spec` when they do not exceed the corresponding QuotaLimit; consequently, the quota’s recorded hard values represent successfully applied claim values rather than the QuotaLimit values.

jip-quota is inspected with `kubectl` to review limits, usage, resource versions, managed fields, pod-count changes, and whether resources are near capacity. It is involved in clean exceeded-quota rejections of pods, including ReplicaSet pods, and may produce HTTP 409 object-modification conflicts when ResourceQuota creation or parallel Job creation occurs concurrently.<SEP>jip-quota is the ResourceQuota expected to be provisioned in a correctly configured namespace.<SEP>`jip-quota` is the resource quota inspected in the `ivan-test-skill` namespace.

entities.name: cloud-console
entities.desc:
cloud-console is a JetBrains-hosted GitHub repository and software project, identified by the relevant source URL and by commit 8c32f67d. It contains the referenced Jib deployment source file and deployment-related changes, as well as the frontend and backend source code, commits, and pull requests. The frontend includes user-management and access-control code. The repository is also embedded as a Git submodule within repos/sre-docs and is referenced by the jbcc-gh footnote.

cloud-console is associated with deployment and operations documentation, including the SRE deployment UI at console.intellij.net, a linked document or documentation area containing the JBCC overview, and a referenced service exposing a JBCC GitHub tab for creating GitHubConnections through a user interface. In these contexts, cloud-console is identified as the deployment mechanism. “cloud-console” is also used as the category and tag assigned to the Terminal page.

As a system, cloud-console contains production and cluster-management configuration. Its production configuration was reported to have an empty destination-principals setting, while its config.cluster-list configuration is used to determine cluster grantability. The system registers both “-eu-west2” and “nebius-eu-west2” as “Nebius (Paris),” likely reflecting differing identifiers for the same region or environment. When Istio is requested, cloud-console creates namespaces and applies the corresponding Istio namespace annotation.<SEP>cloud-console is JetBrains Cloud Console at console.intellij.net, providing a Kubernetes deployment interface using JIB and Skaffold.<SEP>cloud-console is the deployment mechanism associated with LiteLLM.<SEP>cloud-console is a referenced documentation area describing JBCC capabilities for database UI.

entities.name: kubectl
entities.desc:
kubectl is the Kubernetes command-line tool (CLI) used to interact with the Kubernetes API and configured clusters. It must generally be installed and supplied with valid kubeconfig files, credentials, cluster contexts, namespaces, endpoints, certificates, and version settings before use. Successful operations also require authentication and adequate Kubernetes RBAC permissions. Integrations or plugins may be needed for environments such as GKE, EKS, Nebius IAM, JBCC, OIDC, and tunneling solutions. kubectl can be installed through cloud SDKs, runner images, toolkits, deployment systems, cloud terminals, and automation agents, although it is unavailable in the Sandboxed Environment. It does not impose additional JBCC-specific namespace-name restrictions and may function as an external or installed tool invoked by an agent for cluster investigations.

kubectl creates, retrieves, describes, edits, patches, labels, annotates, applies, compares, backs up, and deletes Kubernetes resources in YAML, JSON, and other formats. It supports client-side and server-side dry runs and manages namespaces, ConfigMaps, Secrets, service accounts, quotas, LimitRanges, NetworkPolicies, pods, Jobs, CRDs and custom resources, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Services, Ingresses, CronJobs, nodes, claims, RoleBindings, ExternalSecrets, SecretStores, Kafka, ArgoCD, and other platform resources. It is used interactively and in CI/CD systems such as Skaffold, Make, GitHub Actions, and TeamCity, including for rollout checks, pod queries, and PostgreSQL administration.

For administration, validation, troubleshooting, remediation, automation, and disaster-recovery testing, kubectl inspects live cluster state, events, logs, node conditions, storage, workloads, ingress, metrics, HPA settings, controllers, quotas, annotations, policies, service accounts, and namespace YAML. It retrieves and follows logs, executes commands, opens shells, attaches to containers, launches ephemeral debug containers and restore Jobs, extracts Secrets, copies files, restarts or scales workloads, cordons or uncordons nodes, watches events, accesses raw APIs, and performs connectivity checks. Streaming support enables exec, attach, and port-forward access to pods, services, Kafka UI, Loki, VNC, and metrics endpoints. It can inspect values such as `MAX_NAMESPACE`, `jip-quota`, KafkaTopic status, resolved-entities ConfigMaps, Secret data, host keys, and `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`, decoding base64 values when required.

kubectl can record test namespaces in its local cache, including through an optional namespace lookup, and is used to retrieve current NetworkPolicies and describe the `alb-test` Ingress, including its status and events. Its operation may be limited by missing installation, exhausted quotas, stale kubeconfig endpoints, login loops, authentication or RBAC restrictions, label mismatches, or API timeouts, including in EKS China and GKE. Although widely used for Kubernetes administration and runtime information collection, it is not always the management method for JCP namespaces, and restoration through it may be non-trivial.

entities.name: Cloud Console
entities.desc:
Cloud Console is a company-wide web interface for automations and infrastructure, available at https://console.intellij.net. It provides a Kubernetes API user interface for creating and managing namespaces, Deployments, custom resource definitions (CRDs), service accounts, container-registry secrets, clients, and related cluster settings, with support for exporting and importing configurations. Users can locate namespaces, assign a Google Group as namespace owner, apply the required annotation, manage namespace administrators, and request QuotaClaim increases when permitted by QuotaLimit. It also supports creating PostgreSQL and MySQL databases and viewing available shared database servers.

Cloud Console supports deployment operations, including editing Deployments, configuring the container-image Build Environment field, matching deployment names and namespaces to configuration values, and moving stabilized long-lived workloads to Kubernetes. Its Networking interface creates Ingress resources by namespace, zone, and class. The platform integrates with JBCC internals, TeamCity, Skaffold, terminals, and deployment workflows, and is the preferred SRE deployment interface once setup has stabilized. It includes observability links to GKE namespace cost dashboards and is used to create secrets.

For GitHub integration, Cloud Console is the recommended interface for connecting repositories, provisioning identities, and managing repository connections. It generates ready-to-use GitHub Actions workflows from a selected deployment strategy and exposes Workflow Config values, including the service account, workload identity provider, Identity Provider, and registered service-account details in the namespace GitHub tab.

Cloud Console is also associated with access-control and operational administration: it is listed as an SRE service accessible through the designated country Google Group, and changes made through its grant interface appear in JBCC access logs. It is affected by Google Cloud organization-wide Access Context Manager session policies, including the scopedAccessSettings session-length override. References also describe it as a digital interface for accessing applications from ECS and investigating their operation, and as a console associated with requests filterable by user agent.

In addition, “Cloud Console” denotes the related repository and software project containing backend, frontend, API, deployment, and event-service components, whose current implementation is used to validate documentation. A separate reference uses the name for the Google Cloud Console dashboard for the signing-jetbrains project.<SEP>Cloud Console is an SRE product.<SEP>Cloud Console generates Container overview dashboards that may expose the missing mandatory-label error in PVC panels.<SEP>Cloud Console is a system that generated a dashboard query later fixed after a prom-label-proxy error report.

entities.name: NetworkPolicy
entities.desc:
NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes networking and access-control resource that defines permitted ingress and egress traffic for pods and workloads. It supports pod-label selectors, namespace selectors, and IP/CIDR (`ipBlock`) entries, enabling control of pod-to-pod, namespace-to-namespace, gateway, node, internal-network, and external traffic through specified ports. Policies can restrict internet, HTTPS, managed database, Kafka, and other dependency access while explicitly permitting DNS and approved destinations. They are also used as compensating controls for gVisor or sandbox-pod egress and for no-network sessions.

NetworkPolicy may be included as an extra application-release manifest or rendered by a raw chart. It can be used with Gateway API and to isolate services such as Argo CD, protect manifest caches and unauthenticated repo-server endpoints, and control access to resources outside a platform. It is associated with traffic-control templates, a dedicated Databao production cluster, monitoring components such as `gke-gmp-system`, and connection troubleshooting. Harbor does not create NetworkPolicy resources, although policies can select sandbox pods through standard labels. NetworkPolicy is unnecessary for protecting pgbouncer from other pods when pgbouncer listens only on `127.0.0.1`.

NetworkPolicy commonly governs load-balancer and health-check connectivity. Separate rules may be needed for GKE Ingress/GCE, ALB, EKS internal NLB, and other external health-check sources, including their CIDR ranges and container ports. Namespace-selector-only rules can permit in-cluster sources while blocking external clients, rewritten node-IP traffic, NLB checks, or other node-CIDR traffic; `ipBlock` rules address these cases. Policies may also affect containers sharing a pod network namespace and host-network reachability, and can silently drop traffic and cause upstream failures, though one investigated policy path did not explain complete pod-level network loss when node connectivity remained intact. Incorrect namespaces, duplicate kind/name objects, or ownership by another Helm release can cause deployment rejection. NetworkPolicy is additionally associated with a thread begun on 2025-03-18.<SEP>NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes networking resource that can allow ingress connections to a Pod port from outside a namespace.

entities.name: jip-quota-claim
entities.desc:
jip-quota-claim is a named, namespaced QuotaClaim resource used to inspect and modify quota requests for a namespace, including the object edited through kubectl in my-new-namespace and inspected during an end-to-end backup test.

The resource can be edited or patched to increase requested quantities, including storage, CPU, pod-count, and the gcpprojects quota identified as gcpprojects.kro.run. Raising its resource entries can provide surge headroom and serve as a workaround, provided the requested values remain within the applicable QuotaLimit. The claim is also the quota configuration object queried or patched when requesting updated gcpprojects quota values.

For GCPProject self-service, jip-quota-claim must be raised together with jip-limits. The Quotas page does not read this quota configuration for non-JIP namespaces, so the named QuotaClaim must be inspected or modified directly when applicable.<SEP>jip-quota-claim is the default name for QuotaClaim resources.

entities.name: jip-limits
entities.desc:
jip-limits is a named QuotaLimit resource used to define and manage namespace-level quota ceilings. In particular, the QuotaLimit object named jip-limits in the `my-new-namespace` namespace contains the namespace’s self-service quota limits, including the ceiling for GCPProject resources.

The resource is queried, inspected, and patched when quota settings are reviewed or increased. Raising jip-limits is an administrator-controlled operation, typically performed by SRE, and is required to enable GCPProject self-service. The Quotas page does not read this quota configuration value for non-JIP namespaces, so its visibility or effect may depend on the namespace type.<SEP>jip-limits is the default name for QuotaLimit resources.

entities.name: Cluster
entities.desc:
Cluster is a Kubernetes or infrastructure environment and operational scope containing nodes, node pools, namespaces, workloads, pods, virtual machines, and services such as YT, Hub, monitoring, logging, ingress, and object storage. It supplies compute resources, potentially including GPU node pools with schedulable `nvidia.com/gpu` capacity, and can host GPU workloads and latency-sensitive services. Node counts and per-pool capacity are queryable, but availability may be limited by vSwitch VLAN design, regional CPU supply, or cluster-wide CPU and memory quotas. Nodes may be accessed through SSH, and a cluster can become unavailable following incidents such as the HEL1 power outage.

Cluster is the target and authentication context for `kubectl`, Skaffold, kubeconfigs, OIDC users, Kubernetes Controllers, and Workload Identity Federation. It determines the username used for authorization and scopes RBAC, cluster-wide secrets, quotas, administrator identities, self-service settings, encryption keys, namespace ownership, and permissions granted to created GSAs. OIDC migration environments may expose different RBAC subjects, and changing cluster context refreshes the permission cache. Clusters can be selected in the New Namespace Wizard; registered clusters display a recommended option, Nebius viewers can read them, and cluster-wide edit access permits administration. Self-service configuration and namespace-creation limits are evaluated per cluster, and namespace creation can be enabled within that scope.

Clusters host Helm releases, Deployments, Ingress resources, load balancers, and applications. They support namespace creation, abandoned-resource deletion, workload scheduling, in-cluster tests, NAT-accessed agents, and connectivity to source and destination database servers. They may contain multiple namespaces, such as Namespace X and Namespace Y, and provide the basis for namespace cost allocation using monthly EC2 spending and aggregated resource prices. A Cluster is also the scope assigned to `ClusterPostgreSQLInstance`; an `S3Bucket` custom resource cannot be moved between clusters; and the cluster determines whether a dependency destination contains a pod.

An API Cluster record may include `id`, `displayName`, `cloudProvider`, `region`, `apiserverUrl`, `ca`, `dnsEndpoint`, `proxyUrl`, `capabilities`, and `purpose`. Deployment clusters use UUIDv4 identifiers that seed related UUIDs. Their configuration can define provider-specific DNS zones, required namespaces, role modules, and project associations in `roles.json`, and deployment clusters must reside in the SRE infrastructure Terraform directory. The term may also identify an Office-TV environment, an environment storing `AwsSes` objects and generated secrets, or a service/dependency context.

In observability, Cluster is a Loki label and Grafana grouping dimension, with monitoring narrowed by cluster, container, or Ingress. A faulty Loki environment can affect every cluster in a tenant; one example produces approximately 13 log entries per second and sends 2.3 KB/s. For mk8s, `Cluster` is the `externalTrafficPolicy` value used by `internal-ingress` and `oidc-proxy`; because `Local` is unsupported, client source-IP preservation and the local-only hop are sacrificed. Each cluster also has a separate OAuth client, and only the client belonging to the application-hosting cluster should receive its redirect URI.<SEP>Cluster identifies the infrastructure cluster associated with the database request.<SEP>Cluster is information that must be provided to SRE for a dedicated database server request.<SEP>A cluster is an example of current internal state requiring exact verification.<SEP>Cluster is an infrastructure environment that may be unreachable during investigation.

entities.name: readme.md
entities.desc:
readme.md refers to a collection of distinct README documentation files rather than a single document. Collectively, they describe cloud organization and infrastructure across AWS, Azure, and GCP, including ownership, billing, networking, DNS, IP reservations, AWS China–eu-west-1 Direct Connect, ECR, CloudFront, accounts, WAF, MSK, Kafka Connect, KMS, shared PostgreSQL, Google Cloud Filestore, Artifact Registry, projects, Pulumi, Terraform, KRM management, MikroTik RouterOS backup VPN routers, Identity-Aware Proxy, secondary services, cloud-console overviews, Platform Tenants, GPUs, Istio, application deployment, jb-skills, and jip-controller. Azure documentation includes JetBrains Azure organization and acquisition of billing and cost data, while jb-skills documentation covers installation methods and skill locations; both are dated 2026-10-07.

Other readme.md files document Develocity instances, deployments, access, upgrades, and MCP servers; self-hosted Langfuse, Backstage, GitLab, TeamCity IT, and YouTrack; JetBrains Cloud Console (JBCC), including architecture, deployment, authentication, cluster endpoints, and API-authentication architecture; AuthZ; Code Signing Service; Sparkle Ed25519 signing and codesign; TeamCity OIDC Plugin; and WinCRI, iCRI, and macvm architecture, naming, deployment, VM lifecycles, and cluster-scale details.

A substantial group covers Kubernetes operations and platform components: cluster provisioning and naming, DNS, access control, networking, node pools and provisioners, shared, NAP-provisioned, spot, and GPU nodes, monitoring, deployment workflows, the K8s Component System, kubectl-toolkit, CRDs, and automated or on-demand dump collection. It documents ArgoCD and its hub, Kueue, Kubeflow Trainer, ClickHouse Operator, Glue Controller, Space Controller, KRO, cert-manager, Kyverno, External Secrets, IAM, GitHub, GSA, KMS, Authorization, OIDC-proxy, Credential Rotation, and JIP controllers, including deployment, configuration, specifications, status fields, RBAC, rotation and namespace-creation flows, limitations, ownership, and operational effects. One readme.md serves as an overview index for 18 custom controllers in the repos/k8s-controllers monorepo, while others cover Kyverno chart references, exemption namespaces, and cluster-specific features.

Related documentation addresses KafkaUser targeting, ResourceGrant CRD relocation, UID/fsGroup resolution, policy-name changes, Istio and sidecar injection, Gateway API, dedicated JCP/JBAI gateways, observability-stack architecture and limitations, and GitHub Actions deployment constraints. Additional files cover LiteLLM operations, authentication, access, deployment, support, alerting URLs, Slack channels, namespace-based routing, Database, Kafka, and Object Storage Controllers, including CRDs, cross-namespace sharing, and multi-cluster deployment.

Artifactory readmes describe hosts, MySQL versions, JVM heap, licensing, storage, authenticated channels, image mirrors, infrastructure, and procedures. Other dated materials cover TempVMs, the SRE Product Portfolio Responsibility Assignment Matrix, infrastructure-documentation scope, Skills Index, and the Pier project’s goals, prerequisites, setup, and changelog process, dated from 2026-09-30 through 2026-10-12.

entities.name: namespace
entities.desc:
Namespace is primarily a Kubernetes organizational, access-control, and isolation scope within a cluster. It groups workloads and resources including Pods, Jobs, Secrets, PersistentVolumeClaims, Services, events, logs, and requests. A namespace scopes permissions and operational limits through quotas, network policies, LimitRanges, Istio or sidecar injection, Kyverno exemptions, webhook opt-in, workload isolation, RBAC, Namespace ClusterRoles, alert routing, default quota settings, and user or group permission synchronization. It may be shared by several applications, restricted to a single GCPProject, paired with dedicated node or evaluation pools, or used to scope Workload Identity Pools, service accounts, and AWS IAM roles. Deleting a namespace also deletes the custom resources it contains.

Namespaces generally must exist in the target cluster, either explicitly or during deployment or upgrade; first-time deployments may additionally require Istio injection. They support port forwarding, pod inspection and deletion, log retrieval, restart and status checks, resource listing, and creation of objects such as ExternalName Services, `jip-quota-claim`, `GitHubConnection`, KMSKey, ArgoProject, and GCPProject resources. Jobs and Pods may be governed by batch or JIP quotas, while Deployment Pods require sufficient PVC capacity. A namespace is associated with PostgreSQL and terminal access, runner permissions, and is currently reported as having a 1/1 resource count for `postgresqldatabases.jetbrains.com`. Removing an integration does not affect applications already running in the namespace.

In deployment tooling, namespace is a required or explicit field in Helm releases, Skaffold and Helm-only workflows, JBCC and Cloud Console processes, and EKS or on-premises configurations. It identifies the deployment or cloud-console destination, determines where Helm-released objects are placed, and scopes deployment-status, pod-log, bucket, and Secret queries. It is commonly paired with a destination name, generally avoids unintended use of `default`, and may be represented by an API field whose current value is `default`.

In monitoring and observability, namespace identifies the affected Kubernetes scope and may represent a tenant, release, platform, environment, volume, workload, or target resource. It is used in alert investigation, silence matchers, routing configuration, PrometheusRule validation and channel metadata, and as a metric, alert, Loki stream, log, and event label. Promtail assigns namespaces to matching logs, while Loki indexes and explores them by namespace. Namespace values support target labeling derived from Pods, alert-expression joins, namespace-level annotation joins, routing, service and panel queries, relabeling, silences, Prometheus verification, deduplication, counter grouping, CPU-pressure and ingress correlations, TeamCity consumer results, restart alerts, and refined silence searches.

Namespace also serves as an input or derived identifier for deterministic naming and identity processes, including GSA email and project IDs, CloudFront log prefixes, bucket names, AWS IAM roles, `sts:ExternalId`, ownership identities, and resource creation, deletion, and collision handling.<SEP>namespace is the Kubernetes resource whose creation, quota, annotations, and default objects are discussed.<SEP>namespace is the Kubernetes scope specified when checking whether pods are running.

entities.name: nodeSelector
entities.desc:
nodeSelector is a Kubernetes pod or workload scheduling configuration that constrains placement to nodes whose labels match specified key-value pairs. It is an optional, hard placement constraint used to select eligible nodes based on labels such as `node.kubernetes.io/cpus`, region labels, node types, or GPU-related labels. It can identify a dedicated node pool—for example, through `node-type: my-pool`—and thereby pin a namespace, pod, job, or backing pod to that pool, potentially preventing the namespace from exceeding the pool’s capacity. It is also used to direct gVisor sandbox pods, GPU workloads, and selected components such as `jobset.controller` and `manager` to appropriate nodes, often together with a matching toleration for tainted GPU nodes.

The configuration may be supplied through cluster-specific `_vars`, component values consumed by a chart, or deployment-specific values files, including the `nebius-eu-west2` Kubeflow Trainer and Kueue configurations. It is used on GKE to select GPU models through `cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator`, although GKE does not expose it as a keyword argument; GKE pool names must be used and may differ from Terraform resource names. References to Karpenter pools must be updated if a pool name changes.

In other deployment contexts, nodeSelector is a Nebius-specific setting added to the DCGM exporter. It identifies the node-selection constraint for a backing pod, but does not affect admission-time validation errors and is not supported by `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy`.<SEP>nodeSelector is used for sizing agent pods per node class.

entities.name: ephemeral-storage
entities.desc:
ephemeral-storage is a Kubernetes storage resource representing temporary, per-container or per-pod storage. Its configured request and limit define the amount of local storage available to workloads, and its ceiling must be aligned with the underlying storage-pool capacity. One stated configuration sets the requested ceiling at 50Gi, while other configurations apply ceilings to workloads in the `harbor-eval-intellix` and `ij-air-evals` namespaces.

Exceeding the ephemeral-storage limit can cause a pod to be evicted. This occurred in a build where `/var/lib/docker` used `emptyDir` storage and exceeded the applicable container resource limit. More generally, the resource limit can constrain build and evaluation workloads by restricting their temporary-storage capacity.

In a macOS virtual-machine context, an ephemeral-storage resource request was also used as an input for resizing the VM’s virtual drive. This reflects an environment-specific use of the resource request, while the core meaning remains Kubernetes-managed temporary storage allocated at the container or pod level.<SEP>ephemeral-storage is node-local storage used by writable container layers, logs, and emptyDir volumes, with a default maximum of 5Gi per container.<SEP>ephemeral-storage is the pod-level storage limit that bounds repository materialization on disk rather than the node disk.<SEP>ephemeral-storage retains a 1Gi limit and continues to include storage consumed by the pod's other emptyDirs.

entities.name: CPU
entities.desc:
CPU is a compute resource and capacity dimension used in infrastructure provisioning, Kubernetes scheduling, autoscaling, quota management, diagnostics, and cost reporting. In Kubernetes-style specifications, it is represented through `requests.cpu` and `limits.cpu` and appears as an existing resource type in cluster `resource_limits` entries. CPU usage and allocation are constrained by both cluster-wide and regional quota ceilings; Kubeflow namespaces have a CPU quota of 100, and the cluster-wide autoscaling limit for CPU should be increased together with memory.

CPU was originally used by `custom-scheduler` for node-utilization scoring and is included in SCAD calculations. It is also considered in evaluation-worker sizing, although it is not the binding sizing input, and configurable CPU capacity may be expressed through minimum and maximum requested amounts with a separately proposed CPU coefficient. The VCS pod-scaling HPA identifies CPU as its sole response metric. CPU remained in the normal or low-utilization range during ingress-bandwidth and I/O-bound incidents, indicating that those incidents were not CPU-bound. Conversely, CPU saturation, pod usage, limits, or nonzero throttling can indicate resource pressure and cause latency or stalls even when average utilization appears low; CPU saturation can also signal a problem affecting B.

CPU is additionally used as a wait-event category, including an RDS wait event, for CPU saturation. Infrastructure requirements specify at least two CPU cores and a clock speed of at least 1 GHz, with x86_64 and arm64 hosts recommended for performance. CPU is a virtual-machine resource checked during Windows installation and a category for which hourly aggregated spending can be requested. macOS agent pods request CPU, with one CPU reserved for the host and practical per-pod maximums determined by node class.<SEP>CPU processing supports server queries without requiring a GPU after indexing.<SEP>CPU is an alternative execution platform for dense-sidecar building, expected to be substantially slower than Apple MPS.

entities.name: 5Gi
entities.desc: 5Gi is the ephemeral-storage request value stated for extending an emptyDir volume limit and the threshold for using ephemeral-PVC.<SEP>5Gi is the storage size threshold above which ephemeral-PVC is recommended for fast ephemeral storage.<SEP>5Gi is the default maximum ephemeral-storage limit per container in the described LimitRange configuration.

entities.name: kubelet
entities.desc:
kubelet is the Kubernetes node agent and service that manages pods, containers, node and volume operations, eviction decisions, and pod lifecycle activity. It creates containers, performs readiness and liveness checks through sidecar health-check paths, supplies termination grace periods to iCRI, and can issue parallel StopContainer requests. It initiates pod removal, deletes pod log directories, removes leftover containers through RemoveContainer, reconnects to iCRI to complete interrupted or stale-pod removal, and marks a node NotReady when the CRI socket is unavailable. Repeated KillContainer or KillPodSandbox timeouts can prevent pod deletion, while polling sandbox status may race with pod stopping. It can also kill pods after liveness-probe failures, evict pods exceeding ephemeral-storage limits, and trigger workload restarts through Kubernetes evictions rather than StatefulSet restarts.

kubelet resolves Secret KeyRef values, including `BUCKET`, at container start and retries startup or image pulls when required data or images are unavailable; image retries may continue indefinitely with exponential backoff. It expands environment-variable references and default prefixes, enforces `runAsNonRoot` using numeric, non-zero image metadata when `runAsUser` is absent, rejects UID 0, and does not inspect `/etc/passwd` inside the container. Failed ephemeral-container starts are retried with the same warning event. It enforces pod PID limits using the lower of `podPidsLimit` and `spec.resources.limits.pid`, emitting `PIDLimitCapped` when capping occurs. Resource bursts can wedge kubelet, and memory exhaustion can cause it to die.

kubelet supplies node metrics and PVC usage through `kubelet_volume_stats_*` and the summary API, supports metric scraping and delegated authorization at the node endpoint, and receives `nvidia.com/gpu` registration from the NVIDIA Device Plugin. Scrapes on gVisor nodes may be too slow for Prometheus. It requires reserved memory, uses the configured systemd cgroup driver on k8s-hetzner, and can use `/mnt/local-ephemeral/kubelet` for local ephemeral disks.

kubelet is built, patched, upgraded, and deployed as the node component associated with `kubernetes_version`, including a fresh build for the v1.31 upgrade. Deployment is expected to align it with the fleet; the binary is copied or installed at `/usr/local/bin/kubelet` and restarted after deployment or artifact changes, with the target commit requiring a green corresponding Build configuration. A darwin/arm64 variant is a macOS build containing Darwin-specific process-start-time code and a platform-specific implementation, using the iCRI daemon. It is also identified in logs by the `kubelet` unit label.<SEP>kubelet is idle work running on the E-cores of a Mac node without a VM.<SEP>kubelet is the node agent whose eviction configuration controls disk-pressure detection and pod eviction.<SEP>kubelet is the component that already deleted the missing /var/log/pods/ directory.<SEP>kubelet produces logs showing lost HTTP/2 client connections and failed lease updates for an affected node.

entities.name: GPU
entities.desc:
GPU (graphics processing unit) is a computing resource and graphics-processing capability used across several infrastructure, workflow, and machine-learning contexts. It can be made available to workflow container pods through GPU node scheduling and GPU injection, and GPU scheduling supports machine-learning workloads on k8s-hetzner. GPU is also the computing hardware used by the GPU node pool and the Phase 1 proof, and it is represented as an existing resource type in cluster `resource_limits` entries.

GPU is included as a compute resource in SCAD calculations and serves as the resource context for the cross-account ODCR sharing pattern. Notebook environments may optionally allow users to select a GPU count, while Kubeflow namespaces have a GPU quota of 8. GPU capability is recorded for the `gke-europe-west1`, `gke-europe-west4`, and `gke-us-east1` clusters, and hourly aggregated spending can be requested for the GPU resource category.

GPU processing is generally not required for queries after indexing. However, the `memory_consolidate` operation may use a GPU unless a GPU guard is configured.<SEP>A GPU is hardware that a hosted extractor can operate without requiring.<SEP>A GPU is used by the local extractor provider when running llama.cpp or an OpenAI-compatible server.<SEP>GPU is the compute hardware associated with the required entity extraction endpoint.

entities.name: default
entities.desc:
The entity “default” refers to multiple distinct entities, names, configuration values, and fallback behaviors across the supplied contexts.

In Kubernetes and Helm, “default” is the namespace used when no namespace is specified in `skaffold.yaml`. Helm deploys there, while `kubectl` and Skaffold use it to locate raw YAML objects without `metadata.namespace`. It contains `secret1`, the `secret` and ServiceAccount, the `s3-buckets-lister` ServiceAccount, and the `test1` OSSBucket resource. It was also queried for the `crate-rover-oauth2` Ingress before an explicit namespace was configured.

“Default” is the `LimitRange` name defined in `repos/k8s-controllers/examples/resource-config.yaml` and created in every namespace. The LimitRange injects default resource values, including a CPU limit of 7 and memory of 8Gi, and applies to every `agents-*` namespace. As a namespace type, `default` is rendered on every cluster, is the only namespace type that listed service accounts may create, and is automatically assigned by the Mutating Webhook, or through the `jip.jetbrains.com/namespace-type` annotation, when no namespace type is provided. It is also an allowed quota configuration type, annotation value, and `priorityClassName` value.

In quota configuration, “default” is a `jip-controller` quota profile and one of three associated templates or resource-config profiles. Its `QuotaClaim` and `QuotaLimit` set `count/gcpprojects.kro.run` to zero. In role and extension configuration, it is a special value retained in a role’s `match` list and a fallback extension value used when a required value is absent and `required` is unset; that substituted value is not checked against `match`.

entities.name: MR
entities.desc:
MR, or merge request, is a formal submission of repository changes for review, acceptance, and merging. An MR may propose changes to the `macvm` branch but cannot replace the branch tip until any conflicts are resolved and the request is merged.

In the described workflows, the MR must be accepted and merged before a build is triggered. Merging is also required before Vault secrets can be retrieved and Kubernetes secrets created, and the relevant change must be submitted in the `vault-aws` repository. When no existing merge request covers a configuration change, a new MR must be created, including in the `gke-projects` repository where applicable.

MRs are required for operational and configuration updates. An MR to the values file is needed to increase a namespace owner’s quota, and every quota increase affecting `agents-*` namespaces requires one. An MR in `repos/sre` is required to change a TeamCity internal property. In addition, the ingress owner uses an MR to submit deployment or monitoring configuration changes.<SEP>MR is a merge request from the upgrade cycle that may be merged to master and linked from the SYS-XXXX issue description.<SEP>An MR is a merge request in the cycle that may be opened, linked from the issue description, merged, or closed unmerged.<SEP>An MR is an action outside the shell when it is merged and must be recorded as a timestamped note.<SEP>The MR is the merge request that is not opened until the upgrade branches have been pushed and validated.

entities.name: LimitRange
entities.desc:
LimitRange is a native Kubernetes namespace resource that defines per-container resource requests and limits. It can silently inject default CPU and memory requests and limits when containers do not specify them, using `default` and `defaultRequest` settings. It is referenced in the agents namespace template and is the resource kind specified in `repos/k8s-controllers/examples/resource-config.yaml`.

For ephemeral storage, LimitRange can set default requests and enforce maximum limits through settings such as `max.ephemeral-storage`. One configuration defaults a container’s ephemeral-storage request to 1Gi and caps its limit at 20Gi when explicit values are absent. The enforced scope is per container within the namespace. The cap covers node ephemeral-storage consumption, including writable container layers, logs, and `emptyDir` volumes, but does not limit persistent volume claim size.

A separate jip-controller namespace configuration uses LimitRange to cap ephemeral storage at 5Gi per container. Thus, the 20Gi and 5Gi values represent different LimitRange configurations rather than a single universal limit.<SEP>LimitRange is a namespace resource policy that injects default CPU and memory requests and limits when a pod omits them.<SEP>LimitRange is a namespace policy that injects a CPU limit of 7 when container limits are omitted.<SEP>LimitRange is a namespace-level Kubernetes resource that injects a CPU limit of 7 and memory of 8Gi when container limits are omitted.<SEP>LimitRange provides a separate ephemeral-storage cap for namespace resources.<SEP>LimitRange provides a separate ephemeral-storage cap for a namespace.

entities.name: Logs
entities.desc:
Logs are recorded application, system, runtime, and observability information used to investigate requests, issues, and service behavior. They can provide supporting evidence, explain errors, expose technical error messages, and include raw lines, stack traces, container-command output, and prefixes identifying ICRI or the ICRI agent. Logs may contain a traceID and links to related traces, serve as dependency-specific evidence, support common error handling and custom storage requirements, and provide records for TeamCity Build Agents and TeamCity BuildServer.

Logs can be tailed during runtime, retrieved after restarts, shipped to centralized storage, and queried through logging interfaces. They are collected and stored through Loki, shipped by Promtail to Loki and by Loggo to AWS Firehose, and searched in Loki Explore by namespace, pod, and container. In particular, Loki Explore returns logs for the `confidential-default` namespace; logs also provide the data source for namespace-visibility discussions and derived metrics. Before the event-stream label was introduced, they used `stream="stderr"` and `stream="stdout"` labels.

Logs are associated with backup tasks and controller operations, for which user logs must remain discoverable. They are also treated as node ephemeral storage subject to the LimitRange cap. Container and system logs may therefore have operational, storage, and retention implications.

The name Logs is additionally used for several documentation or interface elements: information moved to a separate article; a link pointing to B’s logs rather than only to caller A; and thread, listing, output, or citation sections containing links only, including a citation linking to a failed build. In these contexts, no quoted log lines are necessarily included.

A distinct related infrastructure reference describes an AWS account with ID 830448721980 in the IT organizational unit that is used for logs.<SEP>Logs include iCRI daemon logs collected from journald and Loki, with timestamps requiring timezone correlation.<SEP>Logs are collected to determine what actually happens and to provide clues about resources requiring inspection.<SEP>Logs are operational data that must be checked before treating hypotheses as verified.<SEP>Logs are runtime information that must be collected first when solving a problem.<SEP>Logs are ALB access records exported to S3 and subsequently read from S3 and exported to Loki.

entities.name: QuotaClaim
entities.desc:
QuotaClaim is a namespaced Kubernetes custom resource in the `jetbrains.com/v1` API group, managed by `jip-controller`. It represents the namespace owner’s requested resource capacity and defines default per-namespace resource count limits. Its `.spec` contains configurable defaults and requested quantities for CPU, memory, pods, persistent volume claims, ingresses, `services.loadbalancers`, PostgreSQL and MySQL databases, `count/gcpprojects.kro.run`, and other feature-gated resources. It serves as the initial quota configuration for a namespace, and its specification and status support reconciliation.

QuotaClaim is projected into the native Kubernetes `ResourceQuota` object: controller logic synchronizes the claim and patches the associated quota, including `spec.hard`. The resource is also referenced by the agents namespace template. Namespace owners may raise or edit the claim through Cloud Console or `kubectl edit quotaclaim`, which can be necessary when multiple applications share a namespace, generally subject to the corresponding `QuotaLimit`.

QuotaClaim values are evaluated against `QuotaLimit`. Although requested values are intended to remain within that limit, a claim may temporarily exceed it, become inconsistent with current usage or the limit, and trigger an alert; QuotaSyncer skips claim keys above its configured limit. In rendered output or user interfaces, QuotaClaim may appear identical to QuotaLimit even when the underlying requested value differs.

Documented defaults and sizing guidance include two buckets per kind, one PostgreSQLDatabase, one MySQLDatabase, and specified limits for pods and ingresses. PersistentVolumeClaims default to `0` against a stated limit of `5`, while `count/gcpprojects.kro.run` is set to `"0"` in all three JIP-controller quota profiles. QuotaClaim is distinct from the `LimitRange` ephemeral-storage cap and is managed as a quota-related custom resource definition.<SEP>QuotaClaim is a namespace resource that NamespaceSyncer creates during synchronization.<SEP>QuotaClaim controls namespace resource allocations required for running the new database beside the old database and for executing backup and restore Jobs.<SEP>QuotaClaim has a default count of one for postgresqldatabases.jetbrains.com and a default persistentvolumeclaims count of zero.

entities.name: QuotaLimit
entities.desc:
QuotaLimit is a namespaced Kubernetes custom resource in the `jetbrains.com/v1` API group, managed by `jip-controller`, that defines hard per-namespace resource limits. It represents the administrator- or SRE-controlled ceiling for resource keys, including the namespace count for `postgresqldatabases.jetbrains.com`, persistent volume claims, `services.loadbalancers`, ephemeral and other namespace resources, and `count/gcpprojects.kro.run`.

QuotaLimit determines whether requested `QuotaClaim` values may be accepted, increased, or applied. It defines the maximum value available through automation or self-service; requests exceeding it require an administrative increase through an SRE procedure. QuotaLimit values constrain claims but do not reserve resources or create node capacity, so sizing must also respect the physical CPU and memory limits of the relevant node pools.

The resource is referenced by namespace templates and quota profiles. In the documented `jip-controller` profiles, `count/gcpprojects.kro.run` is set to `"0"`, allowing no GCPProject resources, while the configuration permits up to 10 buckets and four `PostgreSQLDatabase` and four `MySQLDatabase` resources. QuotaLimit is edited by SRE and may be projected into the native Kubernetes `ResourceQuota` object; changes can cause `jip-controller` to update `spec.hard`. Updated values may remain stale until periodic synchronization. In some user-interface or rendered representations, QuotaLimit appears identical to `QuotaClaim`, making the displayed claim equal to the configured limit.<SEP>QuotaLimit is a namespace resource that NamespaceSyncer creates during synchronization.<SEP>QuotaLimit is a quota setting with a default value of 4 for the PostgreSQL database resource.<SEP>QuotaLimit is documented with default values of four and five in the JIP controller configuration.

entities.name: emptyDir
entities.desc:
emptyDir is a Kubernetes ephemeral volume type that provides temporary pod-local storage. It is created when a pod is assigned to a node and persists across container restarts, but is deleted when the pod is removed, thereby avoiding one separate storage create and delete operation per pod. Its contents are therefore not durable beyond the pod lifecycle. The volume maps a container directory to an initially empty location on the node; depending on configuration, it may use node-local disk, ephemeral NVMe, or memory-backed tmpfs.

emptyDir is commonly used for throwaway Grafana storage, temporary directories for processing large data sets, `/tmp` scratch space, BuildKit’s root, and Docker or Podman data stores, including `/var/lib/docker` and the described Podman store. It is also used for unprivileged Docker daemon setups and is required for `overlay2` when Docker runs inside a gVisor pod. In sandbox environments, it may serve as the default tmpfs-backed storage medium. It can support local build or container storage only for the duration of pod execution and is not a durable repository-clone store; repoServer does not use it for tenant repository clones.

emptyDir usage is charged against node-local ephemeral storage and is subject to Kubernetes eviction behavior and configured limits, including `sizeLimit` and applicable `LimitRange` caps. Multiple directories or mounts—such as `helm-working-dir`, plugins, `var-files`, `cmp-tmp`, and `gpg-keyring`—may share the same limit, including a stated 1 GiB limit. Consequently, scratch data and Docker or Podman storage can consume pod ephemeral capacity. Compared with ephemeral PVCs backed by separate EBS storage, emptyDir is generally slower and may be unsuitable where required data, such as JVM heap dumps, exceeds cluster or node-local size limits.<SEP>emptyDir provides the writable temporary storage used for `/tmp`.<SEP>emptyDir is a storage configuration referenced in the input text.<SEP>emptyDir is the volume type used for the rendered /tmp volume.<SEP>emptyDir is an allowed volume type under restrict-volume-types.<SEP>emptyDir provides a writable temporary directory mounted at `/tmp` by the chart.
