In API and resource metadata, Owner is a reported API-key field that effectively identifies the associated Google Cloud Platform (GCP) project rather than an individual user. Owner is also a default tag key identifying ownership and a case-sensitive resource tag key required to identify a resource owner. For sandbox resources specifically, it is a case-sensitive resource label key whose value must be the resource owner’s email address.

As a query parameter, `owner` represents full redirect-owner email addresses and supports optional filtering.<SEP>The owner is responsible for raising QuotaClaim through Cloud Console or kubectl edit quotaclaim.<SEP>The Owner is the namespace user who cannot debug with kubectl or access the JBCC terminal while quota is exhausted.<SEP>Owner is the database role whose default public SELECT privileges are evaluated.<SEP>Owner is the undocumented responsible party for the external ingress and its allowlist.

entities.name: CRDs
entities.desc:
CRDs (Custom Resource Definitions) are Kubernetes extensions that define and manage custom resources. They may be namespaced or readable cluster-wide by users associated with an authenticated ClusterRole. In the `jetbrains.com/v1` API group, they include namespaced resources for AWS and GCP credential rotation and resources associated with `cluster_type` in object-storage controller configuration. They are also associated with webhook functionality, are referenced in the controllers monorepo overview, and are listed by a reconciler during each reconcile call before being merged into configuration assembly.

CRDs define resources for numerous controllers and operators, including TeamCityProject, TeamCityBuildType, TeamCityProjectFeature, TeamCityVCSRoot, AWS Controller resources such as AwsAccount and AwsAccountAssignment, Strimzi Operator resources, database-controller settings, Key, Grant, IAMRoleSelector, KMSKey, and glue-controller resources. They also support the JIP Quota System through QuotaClaim and QuotaLimit; the Altinity ClickHouse Operator through ClickHouse and ClickHouseKeeper installations and reusable templates; the SRE Helm component; and selected EKS-cluster installations of kafka-controller and kms-controller. Kafka-related CRDs include KafkaCluster, KafkaTopic, KafkaUser, KafkaACLBinding, KafkaACLPrefix, KafkaTopicAdoptionRule, ResourceGrant, ExternalKafkaTopic, and ExternalKafkaACLPrefix.

Operationally, CRDs generally must be installed or updated before dependent resources and controllers. They are required before Certificate resources can be mapped from release manifests, must be upgraded before their associated Helm charts, and should be checked and updated before upgrades. They may be managed through Helm templates, chart directories, Makefiles and values files, or manual `kubectl` commands. CRDs in a chart’s `crds/` directory are created during installation but not upgraded automatically, requiring manual application; some must be re-rendered and reapplied whenever the chart changes, at the v3.0.0 boundary, or once per cluster from a pinned cert-manager subchart. Greenfield cert-manager installations require one-time manual CRD application, while some CRDs—including those covered by commit b4a0947f—are intentionally applied outside the chart. AWS VPC CNI CRDs may also require manual deletion after cluster creation. Kyverno CRDs may be applied out-of-band because nested Pod templates are not always derived by autogeneration and chart installation may exceed Kubernetes’ annotation-size limit.<SEP>CRDs define custom resource types, including KafkaUser and KafkaACLBinding, and may or may not provide an abandon option.<SEP>CRDs are the custom resource definitions cataloged by controller and API group in the reference table.<SEP>CRDs define the QuotaClaim and QuotaLimit custom resources managed by JIP Controller.<SEP>CRDs provide a self-service mechanism for provisioning Kafka resources.

entities.name: backoffLimit
entities.desc:
backoffLimit is a Kubernetes Job setting that controls retry tolerance after failed executions. It specifies how many pod or container failures a Job may incur before Kubernetes considers the Job failed, thereby limiting repeated retries and helping mitigate disruption from unsuccessful batch workloads.

The setting counts failures such as container terminations with non-zero exit codes and influences how many Failed Pods may accumulate, including for a stuck, non-terminal Job before TTL-based cleanup applies. Pod-creation failures do not count toward the limit, even when backoffLimit is set to zero.

backoffLimit is configurable in a Job template and is commonly described with a default value of 6. One description states that it allows up to three retries, which may reflect a particular configuration or interpretation rather than the general default. A CronJob template was reported as lacking a specifically tuned value, so it would rely on the applicable default or inherited configuration. The parameter may also be used in workload planning to determine failure counts and related pod sizing.<SEP>`backoffLimit` is a Job setting whose variation by Job type affects pod-quota sizing and retry behavior.

The policy is an existing baseline policy that additive rules do not remove or replace. entities.name: Generic Ephemeral Volume
entities.desc:
Generic Ephemeral Volume is a Kubernetes volume type defined through `volumes[].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate`. When a Pod using this volume is created or started, an ephemeral-volume controller automatically creates a corresponding PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) and provisions the volume-related storage for that Pod.

The PVC and its associated storage are temporary: they are automatically deleted when the Pod is deleted. Generic Ephemeral Volume can provide temporary shared dump storage and is safe to use with multiple Pod replicas because each Pod receives its own automatically managed ephemeral volume. In Harbor jobs, it may be mounted by step Pods as the `jobs_dir` at `/tmp`.

entities.name: ResourceQuota
entities.desc:
ResourceQuota is a native, namespace-scoped Kubernetes quota object used to constrain resource consumption and quota-tracked writes within a namespace. It stores configured limits in `spec.hard` and reports applied or observed hard values and usage in `status`, including values used to verify enforcement. It may also retain a previous hard value and field-manager metadata, and it participates in admission, deletion, and resource-accounting decisions.

ResourceQuota limits resource requests and the number of quota-tracked objects, including `S3Bucket` and `GCSBucket` resources, regardless of which stack submits the work. It determines whether a namespace has sufficient capacity to create those resources, bounds residual exposure per namespace, and is distinct from GKE’s cluster-wide autoscaling limit. Effective sizing may require checking all three relevant node ceilings. Enforcement can remain at zero when a configured quota claim exceeds its limit, prevent evicted pods from being recreated, and produce HTTP 409 conflicts when quota-tracked objects or KubeDock containers are created in parallel.

In systems using `QuotaClaim`, `QuotaLimit`, and `QuotaSyncer`, ResourceQuota receives projected values after successful claim validation. `QuotaSyncer` updates it after claim changes, enforces configured `GCPProject` or `gcpprojects` limits, may reconcile retained hard values, and can generate parallel-create or per-caller conflict conditions. After a `QuotaLimit` increase, ResourceQuota may temporarily retain its old value until periodic resynchronization; the resulting hard value is inspectable through status. It is also exposed through the quota endpoint for non-JIP namespaces.

ResourceQuota is created by `NamespaceSyncer` as part of the namespace creation and self-service flows, typically under the `jip-quota` name, which verification commands check. It is provisioned after successful namespace creation and is absent when namespace initialization does not occur.

entities.name: QuotaSyncer
entities.desc:
QuotaSyncer is a Kubernetes controller and reconciliation component that synchronizes QuotaClaim configurations with administrator-controlled QuotaLimit values and projects eligible quota values into the native ResourceQuota object, also referred to as `jip-quota`. It reconciles ResourceQuota when QuotaClaim resources change and updates QuotaClaim status as part of the process.

For each quota key, QuotaSyncer applies or writes the QuotaClaim value only when it is at or below the corresponding QuotaLimit. Any claim key whose value exceeds its configured limit is skipped, ensuring that administrator-defined limits are enforced. QuotaSyncer sets keys present in QuotaClaim but does not remove or prune keys that are absent from the live quota object.

In addition to event-driven reconciliation after QuotaClaim updates, QuotaSyncer performs periodic quota resynchronization. Its resync interval is five minutes, or 300 seconds, meaning applicable quota keys are re-evaluated and reconciled within up to that period.<SEP>QuotaSyncer creates QuotaClaim and QuotaLimit resources with defaults and synchronizes them into ResourceQuota.<SEP>QuotaSyncer converts QuotaClaim and QuotaLimit resources into the Kubernetes ResourceQuota named jip-quota.<SEP>QuotaSyncer participates in post-creation namespace provisioning, including ResourceQuota setup.<SEP>QuotaSyncer is a component that takes over part of the namespace creation flow.<SEP>QuotaSyncer provisions Namespace quota after Namespace creation.

entities.name: ResourceQuota 409 Conflict on parallel creates
entities.desc:
ResourceQuota 409 Conflict on parallel creates is a troubleshooting document about sporadic HTTP 409 Conflict errors arising when multiple quota-tracked resources are created concurrently. The issue can affect KubeDock container creation, causing pods to be lost when concurrent updates to the ResourceQuota conflict. The document also addresses conflicts involving other quota-tracked objects and explains why the PVC involved in the workflow is removable.

As a mitigation, ResourceQuota 409 Conflict on parallel creates recommends bounded client-side retries with backoff, allowing quota updates to be retried after contention rather than treating the conflict as a permanent failure.

Istio is a service-mesh platform and associated documentation and configuration area. It covers mesh components, sidecar injection, service-mesh gateways, clusters with a mesh, Gateway API fundamentals, and Layer 7 policy options. Its gateways are fronted by CloudFront, and Istio supports mutual TLS (mTLS), JWT/OAuth-based authentication and authorization, and forwarding of user identity. It is available in the `gke-europe-west4` environment and provides guidance on Istio-related authentication and authorization.

In cluster configuration, `istio` is enabled when the `istio-base` component is present. The `istio` namespace type is rendered only on clusters containing that component, is a valid namespace-type value on applicable clusters, and can be selected through the JBCC wizard. The `buildNamespace` function assigns `istio` as the namespace type for Istio-enabled namespaces. `istio` is also the required gateway class and supports shared gateway configuration.

The `istio` configuration area includes the EKS webhook reachability solution for `istiod`. Separately, `istio` denotes a `jip-controller` quota profile and its associated resource-configuration template context. It is one of three such profiles; its `count/gcpprojects.kro.run` quota is set to zero in both the `QuotaClaim` and `QuotaLimit`, with corresponding templates specifying the same zero-valued configuration.

entities.name: API server
entities.desc:
The API server is the live Kubernetes control-plane endpoint that receives and processes cluster requests. It receives admission requests, manifest-application requests, and rendered custom resource definitions (CRDs) for the server-side dry run performed by ci-plan. It is exposed through the k8s-eqx API endpoint and provides live cluster information, including capability-query responses used by server-side Helm dry runs. Unlike helm template, which does not contact it, `helm install --dry-run=server` can query the API server.

The API server enforces the self-service isolation design and performs authorization for server-side apply requests. It treats server-side apply as a patch operation and authorizes the request before evaluating the dry-run flag. It can also skip a webhook entirely when a `matchConditions` expression contains an error.

The API server applies Kubernetes resource and policy rules during admission and creation. When a pod specification omits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, it supplies a 30-second default. It rejects edits to immutable Certificate domain fields, rewrites `status.used` on every quota-tracked resource creation, and rejects creation of a retry Pod when the namespace’s Pod quota is exhausted.<SEP>The API server is a connectivity endpoint affected by drops caused by the degraded network link.

For a System, `owner` is required at creation and cannot be cleared through a partial update. In generated-key workflows, it identifies the associated team or person.

In dashboard access control, the owner is the dashboard user who can continue viewing the dashboard despite viewer-access failures. In namespace-management workflows, the owner is the identity responsible for creating destination namespaces. In resource-management contexts, the owner is the party unable to self-serve increases to `services.loadbalancers` or `count/gcpprojects.kro.run`.

For affected workloads, the owner is responsible once access is restored, although that owner may become locked out of both `kubectl` and the JBCC terminal. In administrative patching, the owner value is preserved by an administrative JSON patch, whereas a user JSON patch replaces it with the requester.<SEP>owner is an annotation automatically assigned to the requesting user during namespace creation.<SEP>The owner annotation is a managed annotation included in the Namespace annotation allowlist.

QuotaClaim-QuotaLimit describes the relationship between a requested quota and its corresponding administrator-controlled limit. QuotaClaim specifies the value requested by a namespace owner, while QuotaLimit specifies the maximum applied value. QuotaClaim resource values are validated against QuotaLimit; a claim may be recorded as exceeding the current or former (“old”) limit, but it is effective and enforceable only up to the corresponding limit. An alert occurs when the requested claim exceeds the allowed limit, and QuotaSyncer applies a quota only when each QuotaClaim value is at or below its QuotaLimit.

Changing QuotaLimit does not trigger immediate re-evaluation of existing QuotaClaims. QuotaLimit also determines whether a namespace owner may raise a QuotaClaim, and in configurations requiring synchronized changes, QuotaClaim and QuotaLimit must be raised to the same value. In agents-* namespaces, both are rendered identically in the user interface, with values derived from agents_quota; this identical presentation can make the claim appear equal to the limit even though the underlying relationship distinguishes a request from an applied cap.

The described quota examples include a default allocation of two buckets per kind, raisable to a QuotaLimit of 10, and a configuration allowing four PostgreSQLDatabase and four MySQLDatabase resources per quota.<SEP>QuotaClaim and QuotaLimit are combined by QuotaSyncer to produce namespace quota limits.

QuotaSyncer-ResourceQuota describes the relationship in which QuotaSyncer reconciles and projects quota state into the native Kubernetes ResourceQuota object. During reconciliation, including after a QuotaClaim is updated, QuotaSyncer evaluates the claim against the applicable QuotaLimit and writes the corresponding resource value to ResourceQuota when the claim is at or below that limit.

When evaluation succeeds, QuotaSyncer updates the enforced ResourceQuota. If a QuotaClaim value exceeds the old QuotaLimit, however, QuotaSyncer skips the ResourceQuota update, causing the enforced quota to remain at zero rather than applying an over-limit value. During periodic resynchronization, QuotaSyncer re-evaluates the QuotaClaim against the new QuotaLimit and can then automatically update ResourceQuota if the claim satisfies the limit.<SEP>QuotaSyncer projects QuotaClaim and QuotaLimit into the native ResourceQuota object.<SEP>QuotaSyncer provisions ResourceQuota for the Namespace after creation.
